key_insight: This study audits which mental health interventions 41 language models recommend when the same clinical case is presented by a clinician, caregiver, or patient. The supplied abstract describes the audit but does not report its findings.
problem_solved: Mental health advice from language models needs systematic scrutiny, including whether the interventions they recommend change depending on who is asking—even when the clinical information stays the same.
method: Presented 19 clinical case vignettes and five questions to 41 language models from three perspectives: clinician, caregiver, and patient.
Collected 35,055 free-text responses and extracted every named intervention using a validated judge.
Had 29 models rate the full list of intervention options.
impact: For AI/ML practitioners, the study offers a framework for auditing mental health recommendations across user roles. Such evaluations can help assess consistency and inform safety testing before clinical or consumer deployment.
visual_elements: Three role icons—clinician, caregiver, patient—connected to the same clinical case and an AI model.
Audit pipeline: case vignettes → model responses → intervention extraction → option ratings.
Scale dashboard highlighting 41 models, 19 cases, five questions, and 35,055 responses.
Comparison-matrix schematic showing how intervention recommendations could be compared across the three user roles, without implying unreported results.
paper_title: Curbside Chatbots: Auditing the Mental Health Interventions Large Language Models Recommend to Clinicians, Caregivers, and Patients
paper_authors: Matthew Flathers, Jill Noorily, Phuong Anh Nguyen, Mark Kalinich, Mina Fallah
